notes.meaning: God asks Job if he knows when mountain goats give birth, or if he has watched deer calve. These shy animals live on high, rocky crags far away from human eyes. God alone watches over them and protects them when they are most helpless.

God asks whether Job can count the months of their pregnancy or name the exact day they will give birth. Human shepherds carefully track the breeding seasons of their tame sheep, but no person manages wild deer. God alone directs their secret cycles without any help from man.

The wild deer kneel down to deliver their fawns and push through the pain of labor. Even without shelter or help from humans, their offspring are born safely in the rough wilderness. God gave these wild mothers the natural instinct to bring forth life on rugged rocks.

The young fawns quickly grow strong and healthy out in the open fields. Once they can feed themselves, they run off and do not return to their mothers. God designed this healthy growth so that wild herds flourish without human care.

God asks who gave the wild donkey its freedom and loosed it from every harness. Unlike domestic donkeys that carry heavy packs for people, this creature refuses all ropes and human masters. Its love of open liberty is a gift placed in its nature by God alone.

God appointed the dry wilderness and salty flats to be the wild donkey's home. People cannot easily farm or survive in such barren ground, yet this creature thrives there. God faithfully provides a dwelling place even in the most desolate lands.

The wild donkey laughs at the noisy crowds of the city and ignores the shouts of any taskmaster. It is too swift and cautious for hunters to capture or tame. Its freedom shows that God created magnificent things that exist completely outside human control.

The wild donkey roams across the mountains to find its pasture. It searches the barren hills for any green blade or plant to eat. God guides this free animal so it finds enough food to survive in harsh places.

God asks Job if the mighty wild ox would ever agree to serve him or sleep peacefully beside his feeding trough. Unlike a domestic farm ox, this powerful beast cannot be tamed by food or shelter. It obeys no human owner and bows only to the Creator.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars identify this beast as the aurochs, an extinct and massive wild ox that was far larger and fiercer than domestic cattle, rather than a rhinoceros or mythical unicorn.

notes.meaning: God challenges Job to tie a harness to the wild ox to make it plow straight furrows in the field. No human farmer can force this giant animal to follow behind him and smooth down the dirt. God shows Job that human strength is totally helpless before such creatures.

God asks whether Job can rely on the wild ox's massive strength to do his hard farm chores. Great power is useless to a farmer if the beast cannot be governed or trusted. This reminds Job that he cannot even manage an earthly animal, much less govern God's providence, which is His wise and holy care over all things.

God asks if Job could ever trust the wild ox to haul harvested grain home to the threshing floor. A farmer easily relies on a gentle ox to pull the grain cart, but the wild ox would only bring danger and destruction. God gave different natures to wild and tame beasts according to His own wise plan.

The ostrich flaps its wings with joy, but its feathers cannot match the flying wings of the stork. Its plumage is beautiful, yet it cannot lift this huge bird into the air like other birds. God gave each creature its own distinct body and gifts.

The ostrich lays her eggs directly on the ground, letting the warm desert sand help keep them warm. Unlike birds that build high nests in trees or rocks, she leaves her clutch exposed to the open weather. God gave her habits that seem strange and dangerous to human eyes.

The ostrich walks away from her nest and forgets that a traveler's foot might crush the eggs or a wild animal might trample them. She does not guard her nest with the constant care seen in other birds. God highlights how different her instincts are from human expectations.

The ostrich appears to treat her young harshly, leaving them as if they were not her own. She shows no worry that all her labor in laying eggs might end in nothing. Yet despite this apparent neglect, God preserves her kind through His own mysterious care.

God explains that He Himself withheld wisdom and understanding from the ostrich. She acts foolishly because God chose not to give her the careful parenting instincts He gave to other animals. This shows Job that God distributes His gifts as He sees fit, not according to human wisdom.

When the ostrich rises to run, she spreads her wings and races across the desert at blinding speed. She outruns the swiftest horse and laughs at the rider chasing her. Though God made her foolish in parenting, He gave her unmatched speed to protect herself.

God asks Job if he gave the horse its great power or dressed its neck with a flowing, shaking mane. The war horse displays incredible strength and majesty, but no human created those qualities. God alone endowed this animal with such energy and spirit.

God asks if Job can make the horse leap forward like a leaping locust. When the horse snorts with vigor, the sound strikes terror into onlookers. God fashioned this animal with a boldness that human training alone could never produce.

The war horse paws the ground in the valley, eager to test its strength and charge toward armed troops. It does not shrink from combat, but takes pleasure in facing the conflict. God gave the horse a courageous heart that makes it eager to rush forward.

The war horse laughs at fear and refuses to be frightened. When enemies draw near with sharp swords, the horse does not turn back or flee. God placed within the beast a fearlessness that defies ordinary self-preservation.

Arrows rattle inside the quiver against the horse, while spears and lances flash around it. In the middle of deadly weapons and violent noise, the horse stays steady and bold. God made this animal able to endure the terrifying sights of human war.

In fierce excitement, the horse races so fast that it seems to swallow up the ground. When the ram's horn sounds the call to battle, the horse is too eager to stand still. God gave it an intense desire to charge straight into action.

At every blast of the horn, the horse snorts with joy as if shouting in triumph. It smells the battle from far away, excited by the shouts of commanders and the cries of soldiers. God shows Job that this extraordinary warlike instinct comes from the Creator, not from man.

God asks Job if the hawk flies by human wisdom when it spreads its wings toward the warm south. God gave the hawk the natural instinct to migrate toward warmer lands before winter arrives. Job did not teach the bird when to take flight or how to navigate the sky.

God asks whether the eagle soars high into the sky at Job's command or builds its nest on high cliffs because Job told it to. The eagle flies higher than other birds, far beyond human reach and control. It obeys only the natural laws and instincts that God established.

The eagle makes its home on steep cliffs and lodges on sharp rocky crags. Its high nest is like a fortress, placed far out of reach of predators and human hunters. God provides a secure refuge for this great bird among the highest rocks.

From its high cliff, the eagle searches for food with sharp eyesight that can spot small prey from great distances. God gave the bird this remarkable vision to hunt successfully from high in the air. Job could never design such keen sight or guide the eagle's hunt.

The young eagles feast on blood brought to the nest, and the bird gathers wherever fallen bodies lie. God created birds of prey with instincts to feed on meat and help clean the earth. Even these fierce and bloody instincts belong to God's wise ordering of the natural world.
